transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what's been troubling you enough to come in today?

Hi, doctor. Um, I came in because... well, for a while now I’ve been pretty convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. Which is funny because the finance scene here has gotten so intertwined with the arts lately. I was at this gallery opening downtown a couple of weeks ago, and parking was an absolute nightmare. They had three streets blocked off for some local festival, so I had to walk like six blocks in my good shoes. I just bought these Italian leather loafers and they're not broken in yet, so my heels were absolutely killing me by the time I got inside. 

But anyway, what I was saying is... I feel like they're sending me little signals. Like through the event invitations I get, or the specific topics they choose for panels, or even who ends up sitting near me at these dinners. And I know seating arrangements are tough, I actually helped my sister with her wedding seating chart last year and it took us three weeks just to figure out where to put our cousins so they wouldn't argue... but this feels deliberate. I mean, even when I try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence, I just... I can’t really let it go.

Can you tell me more about these signals you feel you're receiving? Do you believe these people are specifically trying to send you messages or communicate something to you through these events and seating arrangements?

Well, I’m not entirely sure what the exact message is, to be honest. I don't have a decoder ring or anything. It’s more just... this heavy feeling that they're trying to point something out to me. 

Like, at that gallery dinner, they sat me right next to this guy who exclusively handles municipal bonds. And municipal bonds are actually in a really weird place right now. The yields are doing things nobody really modeled for back in the first quarter. I actually had a client call me in an absolute panic on Tuesday morning about his portfolio because of it. He’s a retired architect—great guy, he actually designed that beautiful new library annex over on the east side—but he gets so incredibly anxious about any market fluctuations. I spent almost an hour on the phone with him just trying to talk him down while I was trying to eat my lunch. I had gotten this turkey club from the deli across from my office, and they always, always put way too much mayonnaise on it, even when I specifically ask for it on the side. It completely ruins the sourdough, just makes it entirely soggy by the time you get back to your desk. I really need to start packing my own lunch, it would save me so much money too. 

But, um... what was I saying? Right, the seating. I don't know the specifics of what they want me to know by putting me next to the bond guy, I really don't. It just... it doesn't feel like an accident.

Do you feel that things happening around you, like conversations, events, or people’s actions, are specifically directed at you or have special meaning for you, even if others might not see it that way?

Yeah, exactly. That's kind of what I was getting at earlier with the whole arts and finance crowd here. It really does feel like these everyday things—like the panel topics they choose, or the invitations they send out—have this special meaning meant just for me. Like they're quietly keeping tabs on exactly which clients I'm meeting with. 

Which is honestly a huge headache right now because my client list isn't even fully updated in our new CRM software. The firm switched over to Salesforce a few months ago and the data migration was an absolute disaster. Half the contact numbers didn't port over correctly, and my assistant, Sarah—she's wonderful, but she just had a baby, a little boy, so she's on maternity leave for the next twelve weeks. So I've been having to manually enter these phone numbers and email addresses myself in between my actual appointments. And I am just terrible at typing. I took a keyboarding class in high school, but I mostly just played Oregon Trail the whole time. You know you always die of dysentery in that game, no matter what you do? I think I only made it to Oregon once. 

But, um... anyway. Yeah, to answer your question, even when I try to rationalize it and tell myself, 'Hey, maybe this panel discussion is just a coincidence,' I just can't shake it. I really can't let it go. It definitely feels like it's directed at me.
Do you ever feel that random events, like things you see or hear, have a direct and personal meaning for you that other people wouldn’t understand?

Yeah, I mean, I know I keep bringing up the same thing, but that’s exactly what happens with the arts and finance people I was telling you about. I’ll see something—like the specific wording on an invitation, or I'll hear a certain phrase during a panel—and it just carries this really direct, personal meaning for me. Like it's their way of showing me they're still tracking my client meetings. 

And nobody else gets it. Like, my buddy Mark was with me when I got one of those event emails, and he just looked at it and thought it was a standard networking thing. Mark’s actually the one who convinced me to buy those Italian loafers I mentioned earlier. He’s always been super into high-end menswear. He actually gets his suits custom-made by this tailor up in Chicago, and he takes the Amtrak up there twice a year just for the fittings. I took the train to Chicago once for a financial conference, but the Wi-Fi was just absolutely terrible the entire way. I couldn't get any work done at all, and the café car was completely out of coffee by, like, 9:30 in the morning. I mean, how do you run out of coffee on a morning commuter train? It makes no sense. 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, right, the personal meaning. Yeah, even when I try to listen to Mark and tell myself it's just a coincidence, just a normal email or a random topic... I can't let it go. I just know what I'm seeing, even if no one else does.
Do you believe that events or actions that happen around you, even if they seem unrelated, are actually being done on purpose to send you a message or communicate something specific to you?

Yeah, I guess that's exactly what I'm saying. Like, I know I've been repeating myself a lot about the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati, but that's really what brought me in. I'm just so convinced that they're purposely doing these things—the invitations, the panel topics, the seating arrangements—to send me these little signals. It's like they want me to know they're tracking my client meetings. 

And Cincinnati is such a small town when you really think about it, especially in those specific circles. Everybody knows everybody. My sister actually just moved back here from Denver because she missed the Midwest. She bought this little fixer-upper over in Northside, and she's been trying to renovate the kitchen herself using YouTube tutorials. She called me the other day because she accidentally hit a water pipe while trying to take down some drywall, and her whole downstairs flooded. I had to rush over there with a bunch of towels and my wet-dry vac. We spent like three hours just soaking up water. The wet-dry vac is honestly one of the best purchases I've ever made. I got it on sale at Home Depot during their Labor Day event. They usually have really good deals on power tools around then, if you ever need any. 

But, um... sorry, I lost my train of thought again. Right, the signals. Yeah, even when I try to talk myself down and say, 'Look, it's just a coincidence that they seated you there or picked that topic,' I just... I can't let it go. It really feels like they're doing it on purpose to communicate with me.
Do you believe that things people say or do in public—like things said on TV, in conversations you overhear, or in newspapers—are directed at you or have a special meaning just for you?

Yeah, definitely overheard conversations or things in the local paper. I know I sound like a broken record about the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati, but that's exactly where it happens. I'll overhear two people talking at a networking event, or read a blurb in the Business Courier, and it feels like a direct signal that they're quietly tracking who I'm meeting with. 

Speaking of the paper, I actually still get the physical edition delivered to my office. I know nobody reads print anymore, but I just like the feel of it. It does leave that terrible gray ink all over your hands, though. I actually ruined the cuffs on a really nice Brooks Brothers shirt that way a couple weeks ago. I tried taking it to my dry cleaner, Mr. Rossi, over on 4th street, but he couldn't get the stain out. It's a shame because he's usually a miracle worker. He's actually retiring next month and moving down to Boca to be with his grandkids. The real estate market down in Florida is just completely out of control right now, by the way. I have a couple of clients looking for winter condos down there, and the HOA fees alone are enough to make your eyes water. I spent like two hours yesterday just running amortization schedules for this one couple because the interest rates are just... 

But, um... anyway. Sorry. To answer your question about public things... yeah. Even when I try to tell myself that an overheard conversation or a newspaper article is just a coincidence, I just can't let it go. It really feels like they're using those things to send me those little signals.
Do you ever feel that things people do or say—like TV shows, songs on the radio, or things written online—are secretly about you or meant specifically for you to notice?

Yeah, definitely things online, like LinkedIn posts or event pages. I know I keep circling back to this, but it's the whole reason I'm here. It's those same people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. I'll see a post about an upcoming gallery opening or a financial seminar, and the wording or the specific topics they highlight... it just feels like it's meant specifically for me to notice. Like it's their way of showing me they're quietly tracking which clients I'm meeting with. 

LinkedIn has gotten so weird lately, anyway. Have you noticed that? It used to be just for resumes and job hunting, and now it's like everyone is posting these long, emotional stories about what they learned from getting a coffee at Starbucks. My buddy Mark—the one with the custom suits—he posts on there almost every day. He hired this personal branding consultant to help him write his posts, which just seems crazy to me. But I guess it works, because he gets hundreds of likes on everything. I tried to post more consistently last year, but I just couldn't keep up with it. I'd rather spend my time actually talking to clients or, I don't know, playing golf. I just joined this new club out in the suburbs, and the course is beautiful, but the greens are insanely fast. I three-putted like four times last weekend. I really need to get my putter re-gripped. I’ve had the same grip on it since college, and it’s basically falling apart. 

But, uh... where was I? Right, the online stuff. Yeah, even when I try to tell myself, 'Hey, it's a public post, it could just be a coincidence,' I just... I can't really let it go. It still feels like they're sending me those little signals.
